editorial_contributions.text:
For twenty five years Martin Gardner produced the celebrated mathematical games monthly columns for \textit{Scientific American}. Nobody managed to fit his shoes ever since. This is why it has been a special joy to see these columns expanded with a wealth of new results and appear in the form of books. 


This is at least the fifteenth such collection. As Martin Gardner put it in introduction, ``This is a book of mathematical jokes, if `joke' is taken in a sense broad enough to include any kind of mathematics that is mixed with a strong element of fun.'' It consists of twenty essays, all deep and all entertaining. Once challenged, the reader is afforded the pleasure of working on several problems on his own. The reader can then compare his discoveries with the \textit{answers}, that follow each essay. These answers will definitely inspire many readers to do further reading and investigations on their own. 


The readers of the `Four color map theorem' chapter, may wish to study a new proof of the theorem, obtained in 1994 by the group of four mathematicians (one per color ?) \textit{Neal Robertson}, \textit{Daniel P. Sanders}, \textit{Paul D. Seymour}, and \textit{Robin Thomas}. Their manuscript ``The four-colour theorem'' has been accepted for publication in J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B. 


One of the problems asks to cut a given triangle \(ABC\) with an obtuse angle \(B\) into seven acute triangles. Here is a simple universal solution (for all obtuse triangles): inscribe a circle \(S\) in \(ABC\); draw tangent lines to \(S\) that cut off \(ABC\) two acute triangles that contain the angles \(A\) and \(C\); and connect the vertices of the remaining pentagon to the center of \(S\). 


This is my favorite of the many wonderful Martin Gardner's books. Not just young and not so young mathematicians: every curious person should enjoy reading these essays and pondering on issues and problems they raise. One of those is this reviewer's favorite open problem in all of mathematics (p. 123): 


How many colors are required for coloring the plane so that no two points, a unit distance apart, lie on the same color? 


The answer is known to be 4, 5, 6 or 7: a vast spread, especially since the problem was created by a young University of Chicago student, Edward Nelson, long time ago, in 1950. Nelson was 18 years old then!
